Sarvamaṅgalā
(‘one who brings auspiciousness to everybody’)
------------------------------------------
She is one of the aspects of the देवी or Divine मोथेर्.
She is described as of golden hue and is decorated richly with splendid ornaments. In her four hands she holds a rosary, a spear and a waterpot, the last hand showing the varadamudrā (hand pose of bestowal of boons).
She may be seated on a lotus or a lion.

Sāradā Maṭh
(of Dakṣiṇeśvar)
------------------------------------------
The sages of ancient India had given women equal opportunities, not only for higher एदुचतिओन् but also for spiritual evolution, including monastic life if necessary.
Sāradā Maṭh at DakṣiṇeśvarSvāmī Vivekānanda (A.

-1902) had seriously thought of establishing a Maṭh (monastery) for women also when he had established the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् (and the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन्) for men-aspirants.
At the behest of the Svāmī, Sister Niveditā (A.
-1911) (See NIVEDITĀ for details.) came to India from London and established a school for girls in Calcutta (now, Kolkata), in A.

. This school gradually became the nucleus of the later organisation now known as the सारदा मठ् (and the Ramakrishna Sarada Mission).
When Niveditā plunged into the political field of struggle for independence, the school was managed successfully by Sister Christine and later by Sudhīrā Bose. They added a new section to train adult women in various activities such as sewing and needle-work, along with the teaching of academic subjects like Beṅgālī, Sanskrit and English.
Sudhīrā also started an आश्रम (a semi-monastery) for dedicated women workers as also a boarding home for students and poor women. This आश्रम, sanctified by the stay of Sāradā देवी (the Holy मोथेर्) was later named as Sāradā Mandir.
Niveditā had named her school as the ‘Ramakrishna School for Girls.’ However, it was popularly called Niveditā School.
Since she had been initiated into the Ramakrishna Order by Svāmī Vivekā-नन्द himself, her school was legally affiliated to the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन् in A.

.
Gradually—and especially after India gained political independence—more and more educated girls, some of whom had taken spiritual initiation from the saṁnyāsin disciples of Śrī रामकृष्ण, started joining the school to dedicate their lives for self-realisation and service to mankind.
The movement for a parallel monastic organisation exclusively for women, gained momentum when another group of inspired and dedicated women living in a place called Sāradā आश्रम joined those of the Sāradā Mandir. The centenary of the Holy मोथेर् Sāradā देवी celebrated during the year A.

-1954 gave further fillip to their aspirations.
In January 1959 eight senior members of the सारदा मठ् were invested with सṁन्यास by the then president of the Ramakrishna Order and the Śrī सारदा मठ् was made legally separate and independent.
A parallel organisation, but under the same management, known as the ‘Ramakrishna Sarada Mission’ was registered in A.

.
The Sri Sarada Math (Śrī सारदा मठ्) and the Ramakrishna Sarada Mission are run on the same model, includ-ing all the activities, as the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् and the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन्.
Their Headquarters are situated in Dakṣiṇeśvar with a massive and beautiful temple for Sāradā देवी and a building complex housing the offices and living quarters.
They now have several branches all over India and one in Australia.
See also RAMAKRISHNA ORDER.

Sarasvatī River
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda often speaks of the सरस्वती as a mighty river (vide 2.41.16; 7.95.2 and so on) flowing from the हिमालयस् into the ocean (almost parallel to the Sindhū or the Indus river). There are references to it in other Vedic scriptures also such as Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2.19.1, 2) Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa (25.10.1), Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Taitti-rīya Saṁhitā (

.4).
The Mahābhārata declares that many वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् were performed on its banks (vide Ādiparva 95.26; Vanaparva 12.14). The Kāmyakavana (forest) where the Pāṇḍavas lived for some time was on its bank (Vanaparva 36.41); so also the hermitage of the famous sage दधीचि (ibid 100.13).
It seems to have originated in the higher Himālayan ranges and flown through the present Śivālik range of mountains joined by other tributary rivers.
Once a mighty river, as wide as 8 to 13 kilometres, it might have been the life-line of the people up to 3000 B. C. Severe tectonic disturbances might have contributed to its gradual disappearance by 2200 B. C. into a desert.
The modern rivers—Sarasutī and Ghaggar (Himachal Pradesh)—may be the remnants of the ancient सरस्वती.
During the recent years, great efforts are being made to trace its origin and course as also to revive it in some form. Satellite pictures, controlled excavations under the supervision of expert archaeologists, testing of soil sediment and artifacts by the most modern and scientific methods—all these are leading to a positive proof of the existence of the mighty river.

sarūpa-vigraha
(‘an icon with form’)
------------------------------------------
In ritualistic worship vigrahas or icons are used extensively. These may be sarūpa (with form) or arūpa (without form).
A सरूप-विग्रह has a definite form, the form of the deity to whom worship is offered. It may be anthropomorphic or otherwise.
Excessive limbs like four hands, or unnatural features like half-animal body are often seen in them, to denote their supernatural status and power.
The arūpa-vigrahas are the शिव-liṅgas, śālagrāmas, yantras and चक्रस् as also stones of irregular shapes.

Śarabhaṅga
------------------------------------------
Śarabhaṅga was a sage belonging to the lineage of गौतम. He had his hermitage on the bank of the river गोदावरी. He was eagerly waiting to meet राम whom he knew as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु. When राम, सीता and लक्ष्मण arrived at his place, he honoured them with great devotion and then gave up his old body in the Vedic fire. He ascended to हेअवेन् in a divine form (vide Rāmāyaṇa of Valmīki Araṇyakāṇḍa 5.).

Śāradā Temple
(of Kashmir)
------------------------------------------
The शारदा तेम्प्ले of Kashmir—now in Pakistan—occupied Kashmir and in ruins—is an ancient temple highly revered for several centuries. Śaṅkarācārya (A.
-820) is said to have visited it and occupied the Sarvajñapīṭha (the seat reserved for the best of scholars in ancient learning). Kalhaṇa (12th century A. D.) in his Rājataraṅgiṇi (A.
) clearly mentions the existence of the Śāradādevī temple as also its geographic location. Alberuni (A.

-1039) states in his famous work Tarikh-ul-Hind that the शारदा तेम्प्ले had a wooden image of the goddess.
According to an ancient mythological work, the Śāradāmāhātmya, the sage शाण्डिल्य is said to have established it in the place where he had had a vision of the deity.
The dilapidated temple lies at the confluence of the rivers Madhumati and Kishenganga, on the right bank of the former. This place is about 112 kms. (70 miles) from Srinagar, the summer capital of the Jammu-Kashmir State. It is situated at a height of 3350 metres (11,000 ft.), above the sea level. The quadrangle measures 43 metres (142 ft.) by 29 metres (95 ft.). This is surrounded by an outer wall 3.3 metres (11 ft.) in height and 1.8 metres (6 ft.) thick. The approach is by a staircase, 2.7 metres (9 ft.) wide and 63 steps in number.
The temple occupies the centre of the court. It is 6.7 metre (33 ft.) square and is perfectly plane. It was once (in A.

) covered by a low shingle roof.
The sanctum is actually the spot where the Divine मोथेर् Śāradā revealed herself to the sage शाण्डिल्य. It is a stone slab measuring 2.1 metres (7 ft.) by 1.8 metre (6 ft.) and 15 cms. (6") thick covering a kuṇḍa or small spring cavity, from where the goddess had risen and finally vanished into.
On the Śukla-aṣṭamī day (eighth day of the bright fortnight) of every lunar month, the image that existed in the sanctum till the 15th century A. D. used to exhibit some miracles.
During its heydays, a big annual festival with special पूजा and होम used to be held at the temple during the Gaṅgāṣṭamī day (Bhādrapada-śukla- aṣṭamī?).
The temple being a centre of learning probably had a big library attached to it.

Śāradātilaka
------------------------------------------
The Śāradātilaka—also called the Śāradātilakatantra—is one of the best known and the most widely used works of the tantra-group of Hindu scriptures, which deals primarily with upāsanā or meditation (and allied topics) on the various deities of the Hindu pantheon.
Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra (11th century A. D.) is the author. He was the son of Śrīkṛṣna and a disciple of उत्पलाचार्य.
Out of the several commentaries on it, the Padārthādarśa by Rāghavabhaṭṭa (circa A.

-94) is the most important one.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa was the son of Pṛthvīdhara and belonged to जनस्थान (the modern नासिक् in Maharashtra). He was a profound scholar and a many-sided genius. He has, in his commentary, drawn the material heavily from the famous Prapañcasāra attributed to Ādi शङ्कर (A.

-820). (See PRAPAÑCASĀRA.)
The work is in 25 paṭalas or chapters and contains 4500 verses in all.
A brief summary of the work may now be attempted here:
Chapter 1 (113 verses)
This chapter deals with the philo-sophy of तन्त्रस् which is allied to Sāṅkhya and Vedānta. See TANTRAS for details.
Chapter 2 (153 Verses)
Since the letters of the alphabet are the basic material out of which the various mantras are formed, this chapter is devoted to them, their evolution and their varieties.
Mantras ending in phaṭ are considered masculine, those ending in स्वाहा are feminine and the others ending in namaḥ are neuter.
Chapter 3 (135 Verses)
This section deals with Vāstuyāga, erection of मण्डप (small enclosed structure), वेदि (platform) with yantras (mystical diagrams) and होम. These are the fundamental rites needed in all the rituals dealt with in the future chapters.
Chapter 4 (138 Verses)
The first part of the दीक्षा (initiation) ceremony is dealt with in this chapter. दीक्षा is the process by which the evil in the मिन्द् is destroyed (kṣa = kṣaya or destruction) and divine knowledge (dī = divyajñāna) is imparted.
All the details of the ritual to be performed on the first day are given here.
Chapter 5 (165 Verses)
The topics of the previous chapter are continued here.
Four kinds of dīkṣā—kriyāvatī, varṇamayī, alāvatī and vedhamayī—are described. (See TANTRAS for details.)
Chapter 6 (118 Verses)
From this chapter right up to the twenty-fourth, various mantras along with the accessory subjects like ṛṣi (sage), छन्दस् (metre) and devatā (the deity) as also dhyānaśloka (verse describing the deity’s form for meditation), न्यास (ritual purification of limbs) and पुरश्चरण (special methods of जप) are described.
This chapter deals with सरस्वती (the goddess of learning) as the personification of the alphabet. She is described as holding a book, a rosary, a vessel of nectar in three hands and the fourth exhibiting the ज्ञानमुद्रा (hand-pose showing knowledge).
The other deities dealt with are: Ardhanārīśvara, combined form of विष्णु and लक्ष्मी, Jagadīśvarī, लक्ष्मी and transcendent Light called Prapañcayāga-mūrti.
There is also a mention of the wonderful properties of the bitter herb called ब्राह्मी which can enhance intellectual powers when consumed.
Chapter 7 (123 Verses)
The first part of this chapter deals with the varṇas (letters of the alphabet) and their goddesses, Varṇeśvarī and Vāgīśvarī.
Other topics dealt with later are: yantras of the five elements, the Vāgvādinī-मन्त्र (that gives the power of speech) a few other mantras and the rules of conduct for one who wants to worship सरस्वती.
Chapter 8 (167 Verses)
This chapter is mainly dedicated to Śrī or लक्ष्मी, the consort of विष्णु. Other names by which she is called are: Kamalā, Parādevatā and Śārṅgipriyā.
Recitation of the Śrīsūkta of the Ṛgveda is recommended to please her.
Rules to be observed by the sādhaka who wants to worship and please her are given at the end.
Chapter 9 (107 Verses)
The goddess भुवनेश्वरी or Bhuvaneśī is the main topic dealt with here.
Her बीजाक्षर (hrīm), description of her form, the nine goddesses adorning the legs of her throne and other allied topics are also given.
A sādhaka, if he takes the brāhmīghṛta (ghee prepared out of ब्राह्मी creeper descried in earlier chapters) over which her मन्त्र has been chanted, evolves into a great poet.
Some more mantras of the goddess are also given along with modes of worship.
Chapter 10 (123 Verses)
The goddess Tvaritā (one who gives results quickly) is the main topic here. Her form, her मन्त्र and all the associated rituals are described.
Other aspects of the goddess dealt with are: Trikaṇṭakī, Vajraprastāriṇī, Tripuṭā, अन्नपूर्णा and पद्मावती. Their mantras and modes of worship are also given.
Chapter 11 (126 Verses)
This chapter is devoted to the meditation and worship of the goddess दुर्गा and her various aspects. They are: दुर्गा, Mahiṣamardinī, Jayadurgā, Śūlinīdurgā, वनदुर्गा and Vindhyavāsinī.
The rakṣākarayantra (protective mystical diagram) of the last deity is also given at the end.
Chapter 12 (166 Verses)
It begins with a prayer to Tripurā and her मन्त्र which is composed of three parts.
The other mantras of देवी dealt with are those of Bālā and Rājamātaṅginī.
Chapter 13 (151 Verses)
Now, worship of the different aspects of गणेश is taken up. The primary बीजमन्त्र of गणेश is gaṁ.
The Mahāgaṇapati मन्त्र of 28 letters is also given.
Other aspects of गणपति dealt with are: Virigaṇapati, Śaktigaṇapati, Kṣipra-prasādana-गणेश and Heramba-गणेश.
At the end, the मन्त्र of Subrah-maṇya (= कार्त्तिकेय) is also given along with his dhyānaśloka that describes his form.
Chapter 14 (148 Verses)
This chapter starts with the मन्त्र of सोम (Candra, the deity मोओन्). This is then followed by an eight-lettered मन्त्र of सूर्य (the Sun-god).
Other aspects of Sun dealt with are: Bhānu and Mārttaṇḍa (whose बीजमन्त्र, which being very difficult, has to be directly learnt from the गुरु).
The Haṁsamantra (same as Ajapā-मन्त्र) is also dealt with. It is identified with the प्रणव (Om).
Other mantras given are those of अग्नि (fire-god) and Turagāgni or Vaḍavāgni (= Horse-fire, the fire that destroys the created world at the time of प्रलय or dissolution).
Chapter 15 (147 Verses)
Now, the worship and meditation of विष्णु is taken up. The famous dvādaśākṣarī-मन्त्र (of 12 letters) is also given.
Though in paurāṇic accounts, the abode of विष्णु is called वैकुण्ठ, here that term is applied to विष्णु himself since he is vi (= without) kuṇṭha (= limitations).
Then follows an 18 lettered मन्त्र and the description of a यन्त्र.
Other mantras dealt with are those of राम (including a long one called mālāmantra), of हयग्रीव and Varāha. A dharāhṛdaya-मन्त्र (on bhū or the earth-goddess) is added at the end.
Chapter 16 (142 Verses)
First comes the मन्त्र of नरसिṁह in his saumya (or peaceful) aspect which is used in propitiatory rites.
Then is given the मन्त्र of Jvālā-नरसिṁह (in his fierce aspect).
Other mantras dealt with are those of the लक्ष्मी-nṛsiṁha and सुदर्शन (the discus of विष्णु).
Towards the end six yantras are also described.
Chapter 17 (162 Verses)
Viṣṇu as पुरुषोत्तम and his मन्त्र of 200 letters is given first.
Other mantras given are those of Śrīkara (8 letters), Gopāla (18 letters), कृष्ण (6 letters) and काम (1 letter).
The method of drawing the Kāmaliṅgayantra is described towards the end.
Chapter 18 (129 Verses)
Now, the mantras of शिव are taken up.
Śiva is he who rules over धर्म. His famous मन्त्र consists of six letters.
A मन्त्र of eight letters, another called prasādamantra, also of eight letters, are given later.
A short मन्त्र of शिव as Mṛtyuñjaya is given towards the end.
Chapter 19 (132 Verses)
Next comes the मन्त्र of दक्षिणा-mūrti with associated details.
The other mantras mentioned are those of नीलकण्ठ, चिन्तामणि and Khaḍgarāvaṇa.
Chapter 20 (160 Verses)
This chapter begins with a long मन्त्र of 52 letters, known as the Aghorāstramantra.
The अघोर-form of शिव has to be meditated upon as of different hues for different results. For instance, he is to be meditated upon as black for exorcism and as white for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Mantras of other aspects given are: Pāśupatāstramantra, Kṣetrapālamantra and Āpaduddhāra-मन्त्र (of Vaṭuka).
The Vaṭuka aspect of शिव can be meditated upon in three forms: tāmasa, rājasa and sāttvika.
A यन्त्र for averting dangers and a मन्त्र of three letters (of चण्डेश्वर aspect of शिव) are also described.
The chapter ends with a beautiful hymn to शिव.
Chapter 21 (147 Verses)
The work now turns its attention to the Vedic गायत्री-मन्त्र, its व्याहृतिस् and other details.
The different forms of न्यास and ध्यान on the goddess गायत्री are also given.
The famous Ṛgvedic मन्त्र (1.99.1) in the triṣṭubh metre (jātavedase sunavāma somamarātīyato...) is dealt with next. This मन्त्र, if chanted in the reverse order, becomes Āgneyāstra-मन्त्र (a मन्त्र as powerful as the arrow of fire). Its uses in fulfilling worldly desires are also given. Atidurgā, Gaṇidurgā, Viśvadurgā, Sindhudurgā and Agnidurgā are the deities to be appeased in these rites.
Chapter 22 (164 Verses)
Beginning with the two aspects of the Atidurgāmantra—Dināstra and Kṛtyāstra—it gives several injunctions relating to the different purposes for which the mantras can be used.
Ciṭimantra of 24 letters (a मन्त्र for black-magical rites) is also given along with the details of its usage.
Chapter 23 (145 Verses)
This chapter starts with the famous Ṛgvedic मन्त्र on शिव (7.59.12) known as the Mṛtyuñjayamantra.
Meditation on वरुण and his mantra—from the Ṛgveda (7.88.7) known as the Vāruṇī-ṛk—are also given.
A long मन्त्र comprising mostly the letters of the alphabet is given for infusing life into the other mantras.
Some black-magical rites known as ṣaṭkarmas—to gain control over others or harm them—are described towards the end.
Chapter 24 (111 Verses)
A major part of this chapter is taken up to delineate 36 different kinds of yantras or mystical diagrams (inscribed on different surfaces by different materials) for achieving different ends.
It closes with a long hymn to the goddess Ānandamayī who is शब्द-ब्रह्मन्, the basic cause of the universe.
Chapter 25 (89 Verses)
This chapter deals with योग. Various definitions of योग offered by different schools and sects are given first.
Conquest of the ariṣaḍvargas (like काम or lust, krodha or anger and so on) through the eight steps of योग (See YOGADARŚANA.) is recommended.
These eight steps are also defined. However, their descriptions vary from the ones given by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras. More details are filled up under each item.
In addition, the various nāḍīs and चक्रस् are also described. (See CAKRAS and NĀḌĪ.)
Other aspects of sādhana dealt with are: methods of आसन (ways of sitting for meditation); ten kinds of ध्वनि or sound heard in meditation; on प्रणव; ब्रह्मन् in his two aspects of saguṇa (with attri-butes) and nirguṇa (without attributes); राजयोग as meditation on the कुण्डलिनी.
The last part describes the union of the jīvātman with Paraśiva (Brahman).

Sarayū
------------------------------------------
Sarayū is the famous river on the bank of which the city of अयोध्या was situated. Since it originates from a saras (lake) in the हिमालयस् it is called सरयू.
It is one of the seven tributaries of the river गङ्गा and considered so sacred that one is advised to remember it with devotion both at dawn and at dusk. A bath in it absolves one, of all sins.
Rāma and लक्ष्मण bathed here before being initiated by the sage Viśvā-मित्र into the secrets of dhanurvidyā (science of archery).
Rāma is said to have drowned himself in it at the end of his life after having successfully completed the task of his इन्चर्नतिओन्.
It is now identified with the Goghrā river in अयोध्या.

Saramā
------------------------------------------
According to Vedic म्य्थोलोग्य् as depicted in the Ṛgveda (10.108) सरमा was a bitch in हेअवेन् belonging to इन्द्र. When a group of demons called paṇis stole the cows of हेअवेन्, इन्द्र sent her on a search mission. She successfully accomplished the task that led to इन्द्र attacking the paṇis and recovering the cows.
Her two issues—the dogs Sārameyas—were employed as the doorkeepers of यम, the god of death.
Saramā was also the name of the wife of विभीषण, the youngest brother of रावण. She was the daughter of a gandharva, Śailūṣa by name. She helped सीता in many ways in the days of her captivity in लङ्का.

Sarpayāga
(‘sacrifice of serpents’)
------------------------------------------
A याग (sacrifice with Vedic mantras) is a very powerful instrument for achieving any result one wants, good or bad.
The king परीक्षित् (grandson of अर्जुन, the great Pāṇḍava hero) had been cursed by the young sage Śṛṅgi to die by snake-bite, since the king had humiliated the sage Śamīka (Śṛṅgi’s ड़थेर्) by putting a dead snake round his neck. Ultimately the king died by being bitten by तक्षक, the lord of snakes in the nether world.
Janamejaya, the eldest son of परीक्षित् who succeeded him, decided to take revenge on तक्षक and the entire race of snakes and serpents by performing the सर्पयाग (serpent-sacrifice).
As the याग started and progressed, innumerable snakes and serpents were drawn irresistibly into the fire and perished. Meanwhile तक्षक had taken refuge in इन्द्र the king of gods and hence he could not be easily drawn into the sacrificial fire. Knowing this through their power of intuition, the ṛṣis who were performing the sacrifice, changed the मन्त्र to include इन्द्र also! As इन्द्र too started being pulled by the power of the मन्त्र, he abandoned तक्षक and escaped.
But before तक्षक actually fell into the fire, his life as also those of the surviving snakes, was saved by the timely intervention of a young sage, Āstīka by name (vide Mahābhārata, Ādiparva, Chapters 51-58).
See ĀSTĪKA for details.

Śāradā script
------------------------------------------
Like the ब्राह्मी and the खरोष्ठी scripts, the शारदा स्च्रिप्त् also is an ancient script that existed in the Indian subconti-nent. It evolved from the ब्राह्मी script, probably around the eighth century A. D., in the north western part like Dardistan, Kashmir, Jammu, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh.
Alberuni (A.

-1039), the Muslim traveller and historian, has referred to this script as ‘Siddhamātṛkā’.
It was the most popular script for several centuries extensively pervading the areas of north-western India. The entire repertoire of extant manuscripts of Sanskrit and old Kashmiri texts of historical significance are in this script. So also the several epigraphic records discovered so far in this region.
The first printed edition of the famous work Rājataraṅgiṇī of Kalhaṇa (12th century A. D.) edited by Mark Aurel Stein (A.

-1943) was based on a Śāradā manuscript. He also catalogued a large number of Sanskrit works in शारदा स्च्रिप्त् from the Raghunath Temple Library (in Jammu).
This script was in vogue till the 13th Century A. D. It was gradually replaced by its own evolution, the Devaśeṣa, which again gave rise to the modern Gurumukhi script.
The script still survives in the older generation of Pandits of Kashmir.

Sarasvatīpūjā
(‘worship of the goddess सरस्वती’)
------------------------------------------
Sarasvatī, the goddess of learning, is an extremely popular deity with the students. (See SARASVATĪ for details.)
Her पूजा or festival of worship is celebrated in three different traditions:
In Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh it is celebrated on the saptamī day during the Navarātri festival (See NAVARĀTRA.) (Āśvayuja śuddha saptamī, the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja or Āśvina, generally in October).
Worship is offered to a picture or to an image (if available), fully decorated. Books, writing materials and musical instruments are kept at her feet. They will not be used for the day.
In Kerala, the worship is offered for three days (aṣṭamī, navamī and विजय-daśamī) of the नवरात्र festival.
Akṣarābhyāsa (initiation for writing) for little children is performed on the विजयदशमी day (See VIDYĀRAMBHA.).
In Tamil Nadu, it is done on the Mahānavamī or the ninth day during the नवरात्र festival, coinciding with Āyudhapūjā.
In Bengal, as also in Bihar, Orissa and Assam, the पूजा is performed on the वसन्तपञ्चमी (also known as श्रीपञ्चमी) day (Māgha-śukla-pañcamī, the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the lunar month of Māgha, generally in February) in clay image. Books are placed at the feet of the image and an elaborate worship is performed. Later, the clay image is ceremonially immersed in a lake or a river.
This day in considered as extremely auspicious for अक्षराभ्यास for children.
See also VIDYĀRAMBHA.

Śāradā Maṭha
(of Śṛṅgerī)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
If a scientific gadget can discover a hidden object for which it is designed, it is even more possible for holy persons with heightened consciousness—and hence endowed with special psychic powers—to discover places vibrating with holiness. Hence it is but natural for शङ्कर (A.

-820), the great philosopher-mystic that he was, to detect with his uncanny power of superconsciousness, the inherent spiritual power of the place now well-known as Śṛṅgerī.
The story goes that शङ्कर’s intuition was confirmed by his seeing a cobra spreading its hood over a she-frog in labour pains, to give it protection from the fierce rays of the hot sun.
This was the first place where he built his earliest of the four Pīṭhas or Maṭhas (monastic centres of learning and propagation of धर्म), the other three being established later at Badarī (the ज्योतिर् मठ) in the north in Uttaranchal, पुरी (the गोवर्धन मठ) in the east in Orissa and the Kālikā मठ in the west in Gujarat.
This centre is also known as the Śāradā पीठ and Dakṣiṇa-आम्नाय पीठ.

The place Śṛṅgerī (a corrupted form of Ṛṣyaśṛṅgapura) was closely associated with the great sage ऋष्यशृङ्ग (See ṚṢYAŚṚṄGA.), son of Vibhāṇḍakamuni. His story appears in the Rāmāyaṇa (Bāla-kāṇḍa 9), the Mahābhārata (Vanaparva, Chapters 111-114) and the Bhāgavata (9.23). He stayed here and practised severe austerities. He passed away at a nearby place, now known as Kigga, both the places being in the Chikkamagalur district of Karnataka State. A temple of Śiva—called Ṛṣyaśṛṅgeśvara—adorns the place.
Establishment of the Maṭha
Śaṅkara established the मठ on the northern bank of the river Tuṅgā. He built a small temple for Śāradā (Sarasvatī, the goddess of learning), drew a श्रीचक्र (See ŚRĪCAKRA.) on a piece of stone and invoked her presence into it. Whether he also placed an image on it and consecrated it is not known. A broken image of Śāradā, made of sandalwood, is still preserved and worshipped in the nearby temple of Vidyāśaṅkara. This image is considered very ancient.
This temple was once renovated during the period of the Vijayanagar Empire (14th to the 16th centuries). The latest renovation was in A.

resulting in a grand structure.
The Guruparamparā
Śaṅkara appointed सुरेश्वर as the first गुरु or chief to occupy the pontifical seat, generally called the पीठ. He reigned over it during the period A.

-834.
Counting शङ्कर as the first गुरु, there have been till now, thirty seven gurus.

Through Fiery Ordeals
As the मठ grew in size, activities, and importance, it also had to pass through many fiery ordeals, primarily due to the political turmoils in South India. After the collapse of the Vijayanagara Empire, which acted as a bulwark against all dangers, the monastic institution and its pontiffs had to face many serious problems. However, due to the power of their own तपस् (austerities) and the timely cooperation of genuine devotees and well-wishers, all the troubles were tided over.
The मठ at Present
If the goddess Śāradā is the central deity of the institution, the pontiff—popularly called Śaṅkarācārya—is the focal point of the whole system.
He lives in the monastic quarters in the area known as Narasiṁhavana, on the opposite bank of the river Tuṅgā.
It is his special privilege to offer worship to the लिङ्ग, known as चन्द्र-maulīśvara (said to have come down from शङ्कर himself) as also the नरसिṁह-शालग्राम (a symbol of विष्णु in his form as नरसिṁह).
He often tours all over the country on the invitation from the devotees of the मठ. During the rainy season he performs the चातुर्मास्य vrata (See CĀTURMĀSYA.) in any chosen place.
There are several temples in the area of the मठ (as also Śṛṅgeri), the chief ones being the शारदा तेम्प्ले, the विद्या-शङ्कर temple, the Janārdana temple, the हरिहर temple and the Caturmūrti Vidyeśvara temple.
The ancient temple of Śiva—called Malahānikareśvara—is situated on a hillock in the centre of the town.
The following are some of the more important festivals celebrated at the मठ: युगादि, रामनवमी, शङ्कर-jayantī, Narasiṁhajayantī, Vyāspūrṇimā, Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, गणेश Caturthī, Navarātri, Mahāśivarātri, as also the जयन्तीस् (birthdays) and ārādhanas (ascension days) of some of the gurus.
The मठ is conducting a few public service activities also.
There are about 80 religious institutions spread all over the country—mostly in South India—under its control.

Sarasvatī
(‘the flowing one’)
------------------------------------------
Sarasvatī is the शक्ति, the power and the consort of ब्रह्मा the creator. Hence she is the procreatrix—the mother—of the entire च्रेअतिओन्.
Literally सरस्वती means ‘the flowing one’. In the Ṛgveda she represents a river and the deity presiding over it. Hence, she is connected with fertility and purification. Here are some of the names used to describe her: Sāradā (giver of essence), Vāgīśvarī (mistress of speech), ब्राह्मी (wife of ब्रह्मा), Mahāvidyā (knowledge supreme) and so on. It is obvious that the concept of सरस्वती, developed by the later mythological literature, is already here. The ‘flowing one’ can represent speech also if taken in an allegorical sense. Hence सरस्वती represents power and intelligence from which organized च्रेअतिओन् proceeds.
She is considered as the personification of all knowledge—arts, sciences, crafts, and skills. Knowledge is the anti-thesis of the darkness of इग्नोरन्चे. Hence she is depicted as pure white in colour. Since she is the representation of all sciences, arts, crafts and skills she has to be extraordinarily beautiful and graceful. Clad in a spotless white apparel and seated on a lotus seat, she holds in her four hands a vīṇā (lute), अक्षमाला (rosary) and पुस्तक (book). Though these are most common, there are several variations. Some of the other objects shown are: पाश (noose), aṅkuśa (goad), पद्म (lotus), त्रिशूल (trident), शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus) and so on. Occasionally she is shown with five faces or with eight hands. Even three eyes or blue neck are not uncommon. In this case she is the Mahāsarasvatī aspect of दुर्गा or पार्वती.
Though no separate carrier vehicle is mentioned, हṁस or swan, the vehicle of ब्रह्मा, her spouse, is usually associated with her also. In popular mythological literature and pictures, a peacock is also shown as her carrier vehicle.
Coming to the symbology: Being the consort of ब्रह्मा the creator, she represents his power and intelligence, without which organized च्रेअतिओन् is impossible. To show that this intelligent power is stupendous and absolutely pure, she is pictured as white and dazzling.
As usual, the four arms show her unimpeded power in all directions or her all-pervasiveness.
Being the goddess of learning, it is but proper that सरस्वती is shown holding a book in her left hand. The book represents all areas of secular sciences. Mere intellectual learning, without a heart tempered by higher feelings, sentiments, and emotions, is as dry as saw-dust. So she holds a vīṇā (lute) on which she actually plays, to show the need for the cultivation of fine-arts. Then there is the अक्षमाला (rosary) held in the right hand. This symbolises all spiritual sciences or योग including तपस् (austerities), meditation and जप (repetition of the divine name). By holding the book in the left hand and the rosary in the right hand she is obviously teaching us that spiritual sciences are more important than secular sciences.
The peacock with its beautiful plumage stands for this world in all its glory. Since the attractions of the world lead the spiritual aspirant astray, the peacock can actually symbolise अविद्या (ignorance or nescience). On the other hand the swan, which is supposed to possess the peculiar power of separating milk from water, stands for विवेक (wisdom, discrimination) and hence for विद्या (knowledge). Though it is true that विद्या or parāvidyā (spiritual illumination) alone can give us मोक्ष (beatitude), अविद्या signifying secular knowledge—the sciences and arts of the world—need not be and should not be neglected. As the ईशावास्य उपनिषद् (11) puts it, we transcend hunger and thirst through the secular sciences and then alone can we obtain इम्मोर्तलित्य् through the spiritual sciences. It is to teach this great truth to us that मोथेर् सरस्वती has chosen the two carrier vehicles, the swan and the peacock.

Sarasvatīvilāsa
------------------------------------------
The Sarasvatīvilāsa is a compilation of various subjects normally dealt with in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. The author Pratāpa-rudradeva was a king of the Gajapati dynasty, who ruled at Kaṭakanagarī (the modern Cuttack) during the period A.

-1540.
The subjects dealt with in the Vyavahārakāṇḍa which is available now in print, mostly concern the methods of judicial procedure.
The work often quotes from the Mitākṣarā of विज्ञानेश्वर (A.
) and appreciates the views of Bhāruci (A.

Śārṅga
------------------------------------------
The weapons and implements that gods hold in their hands are often given special names. Iconographical works describe them with a definite form and certain features.
Śārṅga is the name of the bow wielded by विष्णु even as Kodaṇḍa is of राम and गाण्डीव of अर्जुन.
In the personified form he is shown as a dvārapālaka (doorkeeper) on the left side of the entrance, usually in the fifth enclosure. He is a napuṁsaka (hermaphrodite) with body in five colours. He wears red garments and carries a bow on his head which he symbolises. His ध्वज (banner) has an arrow on it.

śarabha
(‘the killer’)
------------------------------------------
In the Viṣṇusahasranāma (356) the word as applied to विष्णु is used in two senses: one who shines in the hearts of embodied beings; one who destroys evil persons.
According to the legends recounted in the शैवागमस्, शरभ is a mythical animal with eight legs and two heads, that attacks and kills lions.
When Nṛsiṁha, after killing the demon हिरण्यकशिपु, started roaming about in the forest, striking terror in the hearts of all, शिव assumed the form of a शरभ and killed him! Being liberated from the lion’s body, विष्णु is said to have thanked शिव and returned to his abode, the वैकुण्ठ.
Obviously, this is a story invented by the followers of the cult of शिव to deride the followers of the cult of विष्णु.
The Śarabhopaniṣad (27) describes विष्णु as शरभ who shines in the hearts of the souls and bestows लिबेरतिओन् upon them.
According to the Uttamakāmikāgama (54), a text belonging to the Śaivāgama group, शरभ is a huge, monstrous form of शिव, by appeasing whom, one can destroy one’s enemies.
Iconographical works describe him as with a body which is partly animal, partly a bird and with two heads wearing a big crown.

Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha
(‘an abridged version of all the philosophical systems’)
------------------------------------------
Various systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् have their own basic scriptures, mostly in the form of sūtras or aphorisms. Since they were too laconic to understand clearly, later followers of those schools brought up in that tradition, wrote bhāṣyas or commentaries on the same. These were followed further by subcommentaries to elucidate the subtler and finer points of the doctrines as also the arguments for and against them.
However, for an earnest student who wanted to know only the essentials of these systems there were no brief compendiums or summaries available in one place. This prompted several scholars of the later period to produce such treatises.
The following is a list of such compendiums available now:
Prasthānabheda by मधुसूदन सरस्वती (A.

-1580).
Ṣaḍdarśananirṇaya by Merutuṅga (14th century A. D.)
Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya by Rājaśekharasūri (13th century A. D.)
Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya by Haribhadrasūri (A.

).
Sarvadarśanakaumudī by Mādhava सरस्वती (14th century A. D.).
Sarvasiddhāntapraveśaka by a Jaina मुनि (12th century A. D.).
Sarvasiddhāntasaṅgraha by a Śaṅkarācārya of a Śāṅkarite monastery.
Sarvamatasaṅgraha edited by गणपति Śāstri. The author is unknown.
Sarvamatasaṅgrahavilāsa by Rāmasubrahmaṇyācārya.
Vivekavilāsa by Jinadattasūri (A.

).
However, the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha of Mādhava is not only the best of such compendiums but also unique in many ways. Extending over sixteen chapters, it deals with each of the systems as its protagonist himself would have done. The language is elegant prose, interspersed with appropriate quotations.
The systems treated here are: Cārvāka; Bauddha; Ārhata (or Jaina); Rāmānuja (or Viśiṣṭādvaita); पूर्णप्रज्ञ (or द्वैत); नकुलीश पाशुपत (a form of शैविस्म्); Śaiva; प्रत्यभिज्ञा (or काश्मीर् शैविस्म्); Raseśvara (glorifying mercury); Aulūkya (Vaiśeṣika); अक्षपाद (Nyāya); जैमिनि (Pūrvamīmāṁsā); पाणिनि (philo-sophy of शब्द or sound); Sāṅkhya; Pātañjala (Yoga); शङ्कर (Advaita).
Whether the author Mādhava is the same as the sage विद्यारण्य or another person, the son of सायण (A.
-1387), has been debated by scholars. But no clinching evidence has been offered on behalf of either.

Sarvārthasiddhi
------------------------------------------
The philosopher saint वेदान्त देशिक (A.
-1370) is considered as next only to Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) in the Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition. He was a prolific writer not only in Sanskrit but also in Tamil.
Among the independent treatises on Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta written by him, the Tattvamuktākalāpa is an important work. It comprises 500 verses in the long metre, sragdharā.
It has five chapters dealing with five different aspects of the philosophy such as jaḍadravya (prakṛti or nature), जीव (individual souls), Nāyaka (God) and so on.
The Sarvārthasiddhi, also in verses, is his own commentary on the Tattvamuktākalāpa, elucidating the finer aspects of the system.
See also VEDĀNTA DEŚIKA.

1. Introduction
Whether India has produced many great women or great women have made India great, there is no gainsaying the fact that Sāradādevī, the immaculate spouse of the immaculate godman, रामकृष्ण, was great in her own right. As a daughter, as a sister, as a wife, as a मोथेर् and as a spiritual teacher, she has left an indelible mark on the history of not only Indian women, but also on that of the great women of the world. That an unlettered lady, born and brought up in the rural setting of the India of the nineteenth century could rise to the level of a goddess, adored by millions all over the world, speaks volumes of her greatness.
An earnest study of her life is as fascinating as it is educative, of the ancient Indian values that have shaped its womanhood.
2. Angelic Visitations
In the history of the world, the advent of spiritual giants has often been presaged by strange experiences to their parents. It happened to the parents of कृष्ण, बुद्ध and Jesus in the ancient days. It happened to the parents of रामकृष्ण and Vivekānanda in the recent past. No wonder then that it happened in the case of Sāradādevī’s parents too.
Rāmacandra Mukherjī and Śyāmā-sundarī-देवी of the village of जयराम्बाटी (situated about 100 kms. or 60 miles to the west of Calcutta in West Bengal) were a pious couple living happily within their meagre means of livelihood.
Once, when Rāmacandra was dozing off after lunch, he saw an exquisitely beautiful girl of golden complexion replete with ornaments, in his dream. She put her tiny hands round his neck and announced that she was coming to his होउसे.
A few days later, Śyāmāsundarī while returning from her native village Sihore on a hot afternoon, rested under a बिल्व tree. Suddenly she heard the jingling sound of small bells and saw a dark little girl of great beauty descending from the tree and embracing her. She lost her चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. When she awoke, she felt that she had conceived.
SāradādevīThese two supernatural experiences show that the child that would be born to them later, was a goddess, the former representing लक्ष्मी and the latter Kālī, both in one, since they are two aspects of the same Divine Being.
This is further confirmed if it is noted that रामकृष्ण’s parents too had similar experiences, the ड़थेर्, of विष्णु and the मोथेर्, of शिव!
3. The Advent
The divine girl-child was ushered into this world on the 22nd December 1853, as the eldest daughter of the family.
She was named ‘Sāradāmaṇi,’ रामकृष्ण himself declared that she was ‘Sarasvatī,’ the goddess of learning, come down to save mankind, but hiding her extraordinary beauty, this name also is very much in use.">1 the astrological name—as is usual in the Hindu household—chosen to ward off all evil and bring prosperity, being ‘Ṭhākūr-मणि’ (‘Jewel of a goddess’).
The child Sāradā with her charming appearance and disarming innocence, was the darling of the parents as also of the villagers.
Though she was a little reserved by nature, she liked the dolls of लक्ष्मी and Kālī!
As she grew, she started helping her parents in the household chores and also caring for the younger brothers. Often, she would act as the judge in cases of quarrels and disputes among the children of the village, because of her sagacity.
Collecting the grass for the cattle, helping in cooking were some of the common duties assigned to her.
The मोथेर् instinct in her, which later on bloomed into universal Motherhood, was clearly manifested during a terrible famine that once raged in जयराम्बाटी and the surrounding areas. The little Sāradā would often be seen fanning the hot ड़ोओद् served to the hungry souls who used to swarm her होउसे where her ड़थेर् had organised a community kitchen.
4. The Little Bride and the Great Groom
Hindu religion has placed before man two royal ways of life, each of which, if followed sincerely, can lead to the same ultimate goal of life, viz., मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. They are the pravṛttimārga (the path of activism, the householder’s life) and the निवृत्तिमार्ग (the path of withdrawal, the saṁnyāsin’s or the monk’s life).
During its long history, India has produced great spiritual leaders who were either householders or मोन्क्स्. The solitary exception to this is रामकृष्ण who realised God first and then married, of his own accord, and yet led a life of utter renunciation and total dedication to the service of the suffering souls. He was much more than a householder and a monk, an ativarṇāśramin (one who has transcended all varṇas and āśramas), who could be an ideal for both.
Sāradā was destined to be the divine consort of such a divine सोउल्.
When Candrādevī and Rāmeśvar (mother and elder brother of रामकृष्ण) heard that their dear ‘Gadāi’ (Gadādhar, the earlier name of रामकृष्ण) had gone stark mad, they were naturally very much concerned. At their earnest entreaties, रामकृष्ण returned to कामार्पुकूर्, his native village. To their pleasant surprise they found him to be perfectly normal, the same old affable self.
Even then, not prepared to take any risk, they secretly started searching for a suitable bride, thinking that, that would prevent him from becoming ‘mad’ again. When they were utterly frustrated in their efforts, रामकृष्ण himself asked them to go to Rāmacandra Mukherjī’s होउसे at Jayarāmbāṭi where there was a bride specially marked for him!
[According to an oral tradition, the baby Sāradā, on an earlier occasion, had pointed towards the boy Gadādhar from among the boys who had gathered, as her future husband, when jokingly asked by the village women.]
The search did prove to be highly successful. Everything was found to be not only right but also extremely auspicious, except that the bride was hardly six years old whereas the groom was twenty-three!
The मर्रिअगे went off (in May 1859) fairly smoothly.
Rāmakṛṣṇa then returned to Dakṣiṇeśvar (a suburb of Calcutta) to plunge once again into further spiritual adventures.
The little bride continued her life in the same old fashion at her village होउसे.
5. In Blissful Company
Rāmakṛṣṇa returned to कामार्पुकूर् again in A.

and stayed there for a few months. At this time, he called Sāradā to live with him, specifically to train her for her future life. Being fourteen, she was now old enough to understand things.
Rāmakṛṣṇa taught her, not only how to call on God (how to pray and meditate) but also about the ephemeral nature of the world and worldly life. However, he also took care to train her in the performance of all the domestic duties, including the way to behave with various types of persons.
In later years, recalling this period of her life, Sāradādevī used to say that she had always felt as if a pitcher of ambrosia had been kept in her heart. The bliss and the peace she then experienced were beyond expression.
Rāmakṛṣṇa returned to Dakṣiṇeśvar soon after.
6. Womanhood to Godhood
After the demise of Rāṇi रासमणि (A.
-1861) who built the Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple campus, Mathur (Mathurnāth Biśvās [A.

-1871]), her son-in-law and trusted lieutenant, had taken over the management of the temple as also the guardianship of रामकृष्ण. At his earnest entreaties, रामकृष्ण undertook a long पिल्ग्रिमगे along with him.
Soon after this, Mathur passed away.
Sāradādevī was now eighteen. She was spending her days in the fond expectation of the call from Dakṣiṇeśvar which, however, never came. Unable to put up with the rampant rumour that the village gossips bandied about regarding रामकृष्ण’s mental condition, she arrived at Dakṣiṇeśvar unannounced, one night, in March 1872, along with her ड़थेर्, trudging all the way.
Contrary to her worries and fears, रामकृष्ण received her with cordiality and warmth and even arranged immediately for her treatment since she had fallen sick on the way.
She was now at peace.
Soon after her arrival, रामकृष्ण asked her one day whether she had come to pull him down from spiritual heights to mundane depths. Pat came the reply that her only purpose in her life was to serve him and be of help in his spiritual endeavours.
Another day, while massaging his feet, Sāradā in her turn asked him how he looked upon her. The spontaneous reply was that to him, the Divine मोथेर् in the temple, the earthly मोथेर् in the Nahabat (the मुसिच् tower where Candrādevī was living) and she who was serving him now, were all the same!!
Days passed by, with रामकृष्ण going frequently into his ecstatic moods (called समाधि) and Sāradā serving him and Candrādevī devotedly and meticulously.
One day—known as the Phalahāriṇī Kālīpūjā day—Rāmakṛṣṇa made all the preparations for the worship of षोडशी (an exquisitely beautiful aspect of the Divine मोथेर्), installed Sāradādevī on the consecrated wooden seat meant for the goddess and worshipped her with all the ingredients and ritualistic procedures.
Almost from the start of the worship she was in a superconscious state. When at the end, रामकृष्ण offered his rosary at her feet, symbolising the total surrender of all his spiritual attainments, she was in deep समाधि, which lasted for quite a long time. After coming down to the normal plane of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, she walked out of the room majestically with extreme grace.
This event, now well-known as the Ṣoḍaśīpūjā in the annals of the Rama-krishna Order, marks a very significant stage in her life.
Apart from the rousing of the universal motherly spirit in her, she also, automatically, became the possessor of all the spiritual wealth that her divine spouse had acquired over the years through superhuman efforts. Thus, Sāradādevī, the spouse of रामकृष्ण, became the Holy मोथेर् or just the मोथेर् even as he came to be known extensively as the परमहṁस.
7. Flow of Events
The Holy मोथेर्, hereafter, lived more or less continuously for about thirteen years at Dakṣiṇeśvar with occasional short breaks when she used to go to जयराम्बाटी.
These years proved to be hectic in every sense of the term. Apart from taking care of Candrādevī—Rāmakṛṣṇa’s मोथेर् who lived with him till her death in A.

—she had to do all the work of the household, including cooking ड़ोओद् for the ever-increasing number of devotees of her divine husband, now popularly called Ṭhākūr or the Master.
It was during this period, in one of her sojourns to and from Jayarāmbāṭī—probably during her third visit in A.

—that she had to encounter a robber and his wife in the forest area, since she had got separated from the group and lost her way. Her great presence of मिन्द्, fearlessness and universal love made her address them as ‘Father’ and ‘Mother’ thereby melting even their stony hearts. On learning of her predicament, the couple reciprocated her filial love by taking care of her for the night and leading her to the group the next day.
A severe bout of almost a fatal illness (dysentery) from which she recovered due to the simple remedy suggested by the goddess Siṁhavāhinī of जयराम्बाटी and the unceremonious exit of Hṛday (a nephew of the Master who was also his personal attendant) due to his rude behaviour towards her, are the other events worth mentioning here.
8. The Master Departs
Just as रामकृष्ण, the Great Master, had predicted, his departure from earthly existence was fast approaching. He contracted throat-cancer around September 1885 and was shifted to Calcutta (now Kolkata), to a garden-होउसे at Kāśīpur (spelt also as Cossipore), which was quite spacious and airy.
The Holy मोथेर् also shifted there and took upon herself the duty of preparing the diet and feeding him.
The young disciples under the leadership of Narendra (the future Vivekānanda) took charge of the nursing, round the clock.
One of these days, the Master, intently looking at the Holy मोथेर्, commanded her—in spite of her protests—to continue his work of spiritual ministration.
After choosing a day and time for his final departure, the Great Master shuffled off the mortal coil. It was on the 16th August 1886 around 1:00 A.M.
Though some strange experiences had prepared her मिन्द् for this final departure, she did feel intensely the sorrow of separation. However, when the Master appeared before her in a vision and assured her that he had only gone ‘from one room to another’ she was consoled.
9. Maiden Pilgrimage
To assuage her feelings and divert her मिन्द्, a पिल्ग्रिमगे to वृन्दाबन् (or Bṛndāvan, in Uttar Pradesh), a place intimately associated with the life of Lord कृष्ण, was arranged. Some women disciples of the Master as also Yogen (later, Svāmi Yogānanda) accompanied her.
During this पिल्ग्रिमगे, not only did she feel a sense of utter peace and joy, but also experienced समाधि quite frequently.
It was here that she prayed intensely to the Lord to eradicate from her मिन्द्, the tendency to find fault with others. Her later life has proved amply how this prayer of hers had been answered.
Yogen received spiritual initiation from her here as her first disciple, at the command of the Master himself to both of them.
After visiting a few other places she returned to Calcutta by August 1887.
10. Penury and Privation
Even God made himself a वामन or a dwarf while begging from the emperor बलि. So, begging from others makes one small in the eyes of others. Citing this as an example, the Master had asked the Holy मोथेर् to live in his ancestral home at कामार्पुकूर्, after his passing away, without being under anyone’s obligation.
Soon after returning to Calcutta, the मोथेर् shifted to कामार्पुकूर् and started living there. Except for some paddy grown in the ancestral property, there was nothing else to support her. Rice, without even a pinch of salt, prepared after dehusking paddy and cooking, was the only ड़ोओद् she had.
Later on, she started growing a few vegetables in the backyard by dint of her own physical labour.
Though she was contented and at peace, one thing that often distressed her was that she could not bathe in the गङ्गा river. One day she suddenly saw, with her eyes wide open, that the Master had come there and suddenly the river गङ्गा sprang from his feet and started flowing in torrents! This vision satiated her desire by showing that the Master was everything.
It may be mentioned here that according to the Hindu scriptures, the river गङ्गा originated from the feet of Lord विष्णु in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as वामन (the dwarf).
11. Back to the Metropolis
Her extreme poverty and privation, however, did not last long. Very soon, news of her miserable condition reached the devotees of the Master at Calcutta and they made some arrangements for her comfortable stay. At their earnest request she shifted there and started living there till her final departure from this world.
12. Domestic Entanglements
Ever since the Master’s departure, the पिल्ग्रिमगे to वृन्दाबन् and the privations at कामार्पुकूर्, Holy मोथेर्’s मिन्द् was frequently soaring to great spiritual heights and it was often difficult to bring it down to the mundane plane. But a lot of work assigned to her by the Great Master was yet to be accomplished. So, some worldly peg or post was needed to fasten her मिन्द् to this plane and prevent its flying away.
Through a couple of visions, the Master showed her a girl (whom he called, ‘Yogamāyā’) and asked her to fix her मिन्द् on her so as to prevent it from flying too high or away.
This girl was Rādhu, the daughter of Abhaycaraṇ (Holy मोथेर्’s youngest brother) who died prematurely. His wife Surabālā was stark mad. Hence, the responsibility of bringing up that child devolved on the मोथेर्. Or, rather, the मोथेर् voluntarily took up that responsibility as directed by the Master. By pinning her affection on this Rādhu, the मोथेर् made it a prop for sustaining her life in this world, for the good of the many.
Apart from the responsibility of Rādhu and her mad मोथेर्, the Holy मोथेर् often got involved in the family affairs of her brothers, whose profanity knew no bounds.
Though these worldly ties and responsibilities kept her busy in a way, her spiritual sublimity never diminished, even as the river गङ्गा is never polluted by anything floating in it.
Special mention must be made here of an incident at गया to where the Holy मोथेर् had gone on a पिल्ग्रिमगे since the Master—who could not go himself—had commanded her to do so. There she saw a well-established Hindu monastery where the saṁnyāsins were provided with good accommodation and ड़ोओद्. The contrast between this and the poverty-stricken wandering मोन्क्स् of the Great Master—whom she considered as her children—affected her so much that she prayed to the Master intensely with tears in her eyes to provide her children too with similar comforts. Later developments which culminated in the establishment of the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् at Belur were in answer to her prayers.
13. Spiritual Ministrations
If compassion and mercy are divine qualities, the Divine मोथेर् is the very personification of the same. And, the Holy मोथेर् was just that!
The one who had refused to take the responsibility of continuing the Master’s work of saving the souls, later relented to such an extent that even the vilest of sinners were not turned away at her gate. Anyone who addressed her as ‘Mother!’ would immediately find a place at her feet and feel the warmth of the मोथेर्’s love and the security of her protection. मोन्क्स्, householders, children, fallen women, even criminals, succeeded in finding spiritual shelter at her feet.
Her method of spiritual ministration was unique in that all formalities were transcended and infinite love alone triumphed. The disciples would feel a sense of instant upliftment. Many a disciple who saw her for the first time had felt and recognised her as having seen her earlier in a dream or in some other mysterious way. Instances are not wanting where she has herself called persons and initiated them!
She had to pay a heavy price in the form of physical suffering for her liberality. Her attendants and associates had found her doing जप at dead of night for the benefit of those whom she had accepted as disciples, but who had forgotten even the मन्त्र given to them, let alone practise repeating it!
The Great Master himself had taught her various mantras as well as the modes of imparting them.
14. पञ्चतपस् and Visions
Another important incident of her life concerning her own austerities needs to be mentioned here. When she was living in the garden-होउसे of Nīlāmbar Bābu on the bank of the river गङ्गा (near the present Belur Math, the Head Quarters of the Ramakrishna Order) in A.

she performed the पञ्चतपस् or the ‘Austerity of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’, along with Yogin Mā, a disciple of the Master and a life-long companion of hers. On the roof of the होउसे, four blazing fires were prepared, with the fiercely burning sun as the fifth fire. Both of them used to sit in the midst of these ड़िवे ड़िरेस् and perform जप (repetition of the divine name) till sunset. This was done for seven consecutive days, a superhuman feat indeed! It was again during this period of her stay here that she had a unique vision of रामकृष्ण entering the river गङ्गा and getting dissolved in it. Narendra (Vivekānanda) quickly following and sprinkling that water on a large crowd that had gathered there, was the next scene. It was after this vision that she gave permission to Vivekānanda to go to America. मोथेर् visited it first in November 1898 and again during the दुर्गापूजा festival in 1901.
It was again during the same period—12th November 1898 to be more specific—that she inaugurated the school for girls started by Sister Niveditā A.

15. ‘Mother’s होउसे’
Ever since the Holy मोथेर् arrived in Calcutta for a permanent stay, and started living in the houses of the Master’s devotees—and, sometimes, in houses taken temporarily on rent—a great need was being felt by Svāmi Sāradānanda, (a direct monastic disciple of the Master) on whose shoulders the responsibility of taking care of her, rested.
By raising funds including borrowals, he managed to build a spacious and beautiful building in the Baghbazaar area of Calcutta. It was here that he wrote his immortal work Śrīrāmakṛṣṇa Līlā-prasaṅga (Sri Ramakrishna, The Great Master), the sale proceeds of which were partly used in repaying the loans.
On the first floor was the shrine for the worship of रामकृष्ण where itself the Holy मोथेर् also lived. Her entourage also stayed in the same floor.
She entered this new होउसे on the 23rd May 1909 and lived there till the end of her life.
The ground-floor of the building also housed the office of the Udbodhan, the Beṅgālī monthly journal of the Rama-krishna Order started by Vivekānanda himself in A.

. Hence it has also come to be known as the ‘Udbodhan होउसे’. 3 The मोन्क्स् too lived in the same ground floor.
16. पिल्ग्रिमगे to Rāmeśvaram
On Vivekānanda’s triumphant return from the West in 1897, his old friends, associates and admirers at Madras (now Chennai) pressed him to send a saṁnyāsin to continue his work of spreading the message. Accordingly he sent Svāmi Rāmakṛṣṇānanda (known earlier as Śaśibhūṣan or Śaśi) to Madras where he started a centre, now well-known as the Sri रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् (at Mylapore).
Towards the end of February 1911, Rāmakṛṣṇānanda organised a trip for the Holy मोथेर् to रामेश्वरम्, the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
The मोथेर् stayed at Madras for a few days and also gave initiation. It was surprising to discover that language was no barrier for her communicating with the local people.
At रामेश्वरम् she had the rare privilege of worshipping the शिवलिङ्ग in the temple with 108 golden बिल्व leaves (Aegle marmelos) with her own hands.
She is also said to have remarked that it (the शिवलिङ्ग) was just as it had been established by her earlier (as सीता in the राम-इन्चर्नतिओन्?).
She also visited the Ramakrishna Ashrama (now रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ्) at Bangalore during the same period (March 24 to 26, 1911) before returning to Calcutta.
Later in 1912, she visited काशी (Vārāṇasī in Uttar Pradesh) for the third time. This was her last पिल्ग्रिमगे.
17. Mahāsamādhi
Apart from aging factors, the ever-increasing domestic responsibilities, physical strain of giving दीक्षा or initiation to a very large number of seekers and the subtle taking over of the burdens of their sins (even partially) told on her health adversely. As a result, her body began to show signs of breaking down.
By the time the doctors discovered the nature of the disease known as Kālā-azār (black-water fever), it was too late.
A few days before her final departure, she was found to have completely detached her मिन्द् from Rādhu and her baby, thereby indicating the abandonment of the prop that had held her to sustain her physical life here. Now, none could hold her back from returning to her Master any more!
She gave up the physical frame on the 20th July 1920.
Her body was carried in a long procession and was cremated on the bank of the river गङ्गा in the Belur Math Campus (Headquarters of the Rama-krishna Order), where now stands a small temple.
18. Final Message
Five days before her demise, she addressed a grieving lady-devotee of hers thus: ‘Why are you afraid? You have seen the Master... But I tell you one thing: If you want peace of मिन्द्, do not find fault with others. Rather, see your own faults. Learn to make the world your own. No one is a stranger. The whole world is your own!’
This can be treated not only as her last message to the world but also as a reflection of the quintessence of her life itself.
The first part gives a tremendous assurance to all those who have seen रामकृष्ण, the Great Master, to be free of all fear by that very act. In other words, all those who have chosen to have him as their ideal and strive for perfection through the path shown by him, will be freed from the fears and dangers of transmigratory existence.
The second part gives us not only the method of attaining such fearlessness but also the end-result of the same.
At the outset, it should be understood that this ‘finding fault’ does not apply to those cases where love is the driving force behind it and correcting the person is the ultimate goal, as in the case of parents or teachers chastising their wards.
It applies only to those cases where people find fault with others out of hatred or jealousy or a ‘holier-than-thou’ attitude.
By not finding fault with others—since ‘to err is human and to forgive, divine’—we can keep good human relationship with them.
By discovering our own faults and foibles through calm self-introspection, we will be able to make serious attempts to eliminate them, thereby becoming more agreeable to others. Also, we will look upon others with greater sympathy and understanding.
Behind the golden advice that none is a stranger and that the whole world is our own, is the great Vedāntic truth taught by numberless sages over several millennia! If the same आत्मन् (the Self) or God dwells in the hearts of all including myself, then, finding fault with others will tantamount to abusing myself! Once this truth is discovered or the deep conviction developed, the entire gamut of human relationships gets transmuted to a higher plane!
True, this is not that easy as we may imagine. But, by trying to learn to practise it we gradually elevate ourselves—and others—in the truly spiritual sense.
A मोथेर् never sees the infirmities of her children. Even if she does, she makes light of them.
Then what to speak of the Universal मोथेर्, the मोथेर् of all mothers! She who could melt the hearts of the robber couple or make a hardened criminal like Amzad (a Muslim labourer, notorious for his nefarious activities) behave like a loving son, only she could deliver such a unique message, since she had attained to the status of the Universal or the Divine मोथेर् and reflected it in every word and act of hers.
The world at large is yet to learn and act on her message.
19. Epilogue
If the motherly love inhabiting the hearts of all the mothers in the world were to be put together and churned, the nectar that would issue forth would perhaps approximate to Sāradādevī. रामकृष्ण left her in this world to uphold the highest ideal of universal motherhood.
Her rare insight into the problems of Indian women who were handicapped by obsolescent social customs on the one side, and, exposure to the modern Western culture on the other, made her recognise the need for their एदुचतिओन् and even economic independence. That is why she was an ardent supporter of Sister Niveditā’s (A.

-1911) endeavours in the field of educating Indian women.
She is certainly the best bridge between the ancient and the modern ideals of Indian womanhood, retaining the best of both.

Sarvamūla
(‘essence or root of all [scriptures]’)
------------------------------------------
All the 37 works of मध्वाचार्य (A.

-1317) exhibit a thorough unity of purpose. Each work serves as an interpretation of the others. Hence his immediate followers collected his works under a single title, the Sarvamūla.
They are generally divided into seven groups: Gītāprasthāna; Upaniṣatprasthāna; Sūtraprasthāna; Ṛkprasthāna; इतिहास and Purāna; Daśaprakaraṇas; Tantrasāra and Stotras.
See also DVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA and MADHVĀCĀRYA.

sarvaprāyaścitta
(‘universal expiation’)
------------------------------------------
This is a special omnibus type of expiation prescribed for a dying person to ward off the effects of all sins that might have been committed knowingly or unknowingly.
It may be performed either by the person himself or his son or any other close relative.
This rite includes the following steps: shaving, bath, drinking पञ्चगव्य (See PAÑCAGAVYA.), honouring a ब्राह्मण of pure life, gifting a cow or money after referring to the various types of sins he might have committed. This may be followed by further gifts known as daśādānas (ten kinds of dānas or gifts) and the recitation of the Kāmastuti (Atharvaveda 3.29.7; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa

.9).
The whole procedure has been described in the work Antyakarmadīpikā of Haribhaṭṭadīkṣita.
If the person takes āturasaṁnyāsa, there is no need for any expiation (See ĀTURASAṀNYĀSA.).
